target_customer: Universities, companies and landlords buying a bike sharing system, and riders paying per use or by membership
problem: Conventional bike share needed expensive docking stations and months of setup. viaCycle bikes lock to ordinary bike racks, so a system could launch in days at lower cost.
business_model: Hardware and software sold to institutions at roughly 1,000 to 1,500 dollars upfront per bike plus about 20 dollars per bike per month, and consumer fees

founders.name: Kyle Azevedo
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (2012) says the co-founders met at Georgia Tech; Atlanta Magazine and Georgia Tech coverage also appeared in search.

founders.name: Sid Doshi
founders.background_notes: YC page: software developer and mechanical engineer, later Google, Homejoy early engineer; the order relative to viaCycle is not stated.

competitors.name: Alta Bicycle Share
competitors.what: Full service bike share operator, finalist for Portland's roughly 4 million dollar system

competitors.name: B-cycle
competitors.what: Bike share kiosks and bikes formed in 2008 by Trek, Humana and Crispin Porter + Bogusky

technical_complexity.rationale: Custom lock hardware, bikes and software that work without docks needed mechanical, embedded and cloud work by a four person team.

defensibility.rationale: Dockless style locking was a cost advantage but could be copied, and contracts with universities were small.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Large dockless players such as Spin, Bird and Lime appeared around 2017 to 2018. No acquisition of viaCycle was found.

market_need_then: Bike share systems in US cities were expanding in 2012, and TechCrunch notes existing systems were expensive and depended on docking stations. viaCycle had 40 bikes at Georgia Tech and planned George Mason in fall 2012.

branding.community_and_virality: Press in TechCrunch, NBC News and Entrepreneur in 2012 about the startup concept.

brand_strength.rationale: Solid early press about the idea, but no source discusses the brand itself, and it later appears only in a student capstone page.

outcome_analysis: viaCycle built low cost dockless style bike share for campuses, with 40 bikes at Georgia Tech in 2012 and later systems at George Mason and Las Vegas per a 2015 student page. The YC directory marks it Inactive with no date, and no shutdown or acquisition report was found, so the cause is not public. Raised funding appears small, about 90 thousand dollars per one database, so the market and capital are context rather than a documented cause.
notes: viacycle.com returned HTTP 503.
